Dave wrote the first line in his notebook. It says: they can see my shirt.
Is that real? Partly. In two thousand four, the biologist Con Slobodchikoff and two colleagues tested it in a colony of Gunnison's prairie dogs in Arizona.
Three women of similar height walked through the colony ninety-nine times in total.
All three wore blue jeans and sunglasses. The only thing that changed was the colour of the shirt: blue, green or yellow.
It is the most consistent outfit in science.
They recorded eighty-two alarm calls from forty-eight marked animals. Then a computer measured the sound of each call.
The calls for blue and for yellow were different, and so were the calls for blue and for green. But the calls for green and for yellow were not.
The authors said that fits how prairie dogs see. They suggested the animals build labels for a predator's features into their calls.
It was not perfect. The computer guessed the shirt from the call about fifty-five percent of the time. Chance would be thirty-three.
In a later study, the calls also differed for cut-out shapes of different sizes, like a circle, a square and a triangle.
This isn't new. Prairie dogs already have different calls for a hawk, a human, a coyote and a domestic dog.
And in nineteen eighty, researchers showed vervet monkeys have different calls for a leopard, an eagle and a python.
So a prairie dog has four ways of saying something is going to eat me, and one of them is human.
Researchers use a careful term for this: functional reference.
The call works as if it refers to the predator, but proving what the animal means is hard. The prairie dog is not available for comment.
Dave looks at the notebook. They can tell blue from yellow. It is not a secret. It is a shirt.
Next, the bees. Karl von Frisch decoded their dance using glass-walled hives. It won him a share of the Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three.
A bee that finds food flies back and dances.
In the dark hive, gravity stands in for the Sun. The angle of its waggle run, measured from straight up,
shows where the food is compared with the Sun.
The length of the run shows the distance. A run lasting two and a half seconds means roughly two thousand six hundred metres.
If the flowers are within about fifty metres, the bee dances in a circle. That says close to the hive, but gives no direction.
Dave asks a bee what the meaning of life is.
Two and a half seconds, that way, near the Sun. Please move.

It is one of the most precise animal messages we have decoded. And it is a set of directions to some flowers.
When a swarm needs a new home, hundreds of scouts dance for different sites.
In twenty eleven, researchers found a signal nobody had noticed: a very short buzz, delivered while head-butting a dancer.
It shortens and ends the dance.
Bees settle a disagreement with a buzz and a head-butt. No further questions.
Dave writes in the notebook: bees give better directions than I do.
But do animals ever say who is who?
In twenty thirteen, researchers at the University of St Andrews played computer copies of signature whistles to wild bottlenose dolphins off the coast of Scotland.
Each dolphin reacted only when it heard the copy of its own whistle. One of the authors called it the first case of naming in mammals.
We had assumed names were ours. Nobody had asked the dolphins.
In twenty twenty-four, a team recorded wild elephants in Kenya.
A computer model trained on four hundred and thirty-seven calls from ninety-nine callers could name the recipient of about a quarter of calls it had never heard.
Not a translator yet. A decent guesser.
Then they played calls to seventeen elephants. An elephant approached the speaker, on average, a hundred and twenty-eight seconds sooner when the call had been addressed to it.
The same year, a team in Israel showed that marmoset monkeys use special calls to label each other, and answer more accurately when called.
Families seem to share a similar style, like a dialect.
The elephant team was careful. The model might have picked up each caller's voice, and they are not sure where the name sits inside a call.
So at least four species seem to label each other: humans, dolphins, elephants and marmosets.

In twenty eleven, researchers at Wofford College reported that a border collie named Chaser had learned the names of one thousand and twenty-two objects over three years of training.
She could even learn a new name by elimination. Given one unfamiliar toy among familiar ones, she picked it when she heard an unfamiliar word.
The authors said this kind of understanding is normally credited to children.
She understood a thousand and twenty-two words. She said none of them back.
Now the hard one. Sperm whales make patterns of short bursts of clicks called codas.
In twenty twenty-four, a team led from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology analysed nearly nine thousand codas from whales off the island of Dominica.
They found that codas combine four features: rhythm, tempo, and two finer features they named rubato and ornamentation.
These can be mixed freely into a large set of distinct codas.
Some compared it to a phonetic alphabet. But the project's leaders were careful. One said the meaning of many codas remains unknown.
So the whales have an alphabet with no dictionary.
Dave asks a whale what a coda means. It replies with a little rubato.

In May twenty twenty-four, a foundation and Tel Aviv University launched a challenge worth up to ten million dollars for talking with another species.
The grand prize needs a kind of Turing test: the animal has to communicate independently, without recognising that it is communicating with humans.
A prairie dog would never pass. It announces the human before the human arrives.
There is also a hundred thousand dollar prize every year for the best progress.
Four finalists in twenty twenty-five, from the United States, Germany, France and Israel, were working with dolphins, nightingales, cuttlefish and monkeys.
